standard.title: Places of Significance and Australian Experiences in WWI
standard.description: the places of significance where Australians fought, their perspectives and experiences, including the Gallipoli campaign, the Western Front and the Middle East
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have studied the causes of WWI and Australian enlistment (AC9HH9K08). They understand why Australians went to war and what motivated them. They have not yet examined where Australians fought, the conditions of different theatres of war, or how the experience of combat varied by location and role.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students identify the places of significance where Australians fought, and examine the perspectives and experiences of soldiers in different theatres of the war.

nodes.label: Places where Australians fought
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the major places where Australians fought in WWI and describe their geographic and strategic context.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least four places where Australians fought in WWI and locate them geographically.
nodes.typical_width: Identify the places where Australians fought: Gallipoli; Western Front (Fromelles, the Somme, Pozières, Passchendaele, Bullecourt, Villers-Bretonneux); Middle East/North Africa (Sinai Peninsula, Gaza, Beersheba); describe the geographic and strategic context of each major theatre.
wider: Map all major Australian battle sites and examine the strategic logic connecting them — analysing how the war's geography changed from Gallipoli (amphibious assault, failed campaign) to the Western Front (industrial attrition) to the Middle East (mobile cavalry warfare)
Investigate one less well-known Australian campaign (e.g. Fromelles or Bullecourt) to examine how battles outside the 'iconic' narrative (Gallipoli, Beersheba) shaped the Australian WWI experience

response_modes.reason: Geographic knowledge of where Australians fought is a necessary foundation before examining the conditions and experiences at those locations. Accurate place-knowledge supports all subsequent analysis.

success_criteria: Identifies at least five places where Australians fought in WWI, correctly located in the correct theatre
Describes the geographic context of at least two major theatres (Western Front, Gallipoli, Middle East)

nodes.label: Conditions and technology of trench warfare
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate the difficulties of trench warfare and explain how the development of new military technology changed the nature of combat.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least two difficulties of trench warfare and identify one new military technology used in WWI.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate the difficulties of trench warfare — mud, disease, shelling, 'going over the top', shell shock; examine the development and impact of new military technologies including tanks, aeroplanes, and chemical weapons (gas); explain how these technologies changed the nature of warfare and the experience of soldiers.
wider: Examine the development of chemical warfare (gas) as a case study in how technology can violate established rules of war — and investigate how the international community responded to its use
Investigate how the tank changed tactical thinking on the Western Front — examining specific battles (e.g. Cambrai, 1917) where tanks were used to break the trench deadlock

Examine shell shock (now understood as PTSD) as evidence that the psychological impact of industrial warfare was not adequately understood or addressed — connecting historical conditions to contemporary understanding of trauma

response_modes.reason: Examining both physical conditions (mud, disease, shelling) and technological change (tanks, gas, aeroplanes) gives a fuller picture of what made WWI a different kind of war — the technological dimension is often reduced to 'guns' if not explicitly taught.

success_criteria: Describes at least three difficulties of trench warfare drawing on specific conditions
Identifies at least two new military technologies and explains how each changed the experience or nature of combat

nodes.label: Comparing experiences across theatres — Western Front vs Middle East
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare and contrast the different experiences of war across at least two theatres, including the experience of Australian soldiers in different roles and locations.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare the experience of soldiers in one Western Front battle with one Middle East campaign, identifying at least two differences.
nodes.typical_width: Compare and contrast the different experiences of war including foot soldiers on the Western Front (industrial attrition, trench warfare, mud, gas, constant shelling) versus Light Horse in Palestine (mobile cavalry warfare, desert conditions, different tactical demands); examine how location and role shaped the soldier's experience of war.
wider: Examine the experiences of First Nations Australian soldiers in specific campaigns — identifying how racial identity shaped their assignments, treatment by officers, and post-war recognition
Compare the experiences of officers and enlisted soldiers in the same campaign to examine how rank and class shaped the WWI experience
Investigate the experiences of Australian nurses or other non-combat roles to examine dimensions of the war experience not captured by combat-focused narratives

response_modes.reason: Using both Western Front and Middle East examples, and examining multiple roles, prevents students from reducing Australian WWI experience to a single type (usually Gallipoli) and develops genuinely comparative historical thinking.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The contrast between different theatres and roles is pedagogically rich — it reveals how 'the war' was not a single experience but multiple distinct conditions that produced very different soldier perspectives. The Light Horse in Palestine is often underemphasised and offers genuine contrast with Western Front narratives.
success_criteria: Compares the experiences of soldiers in at least two different theatres or roles, identifying specific differences in conditions and demands
Explains how location and role shaped the nature of soldiers' wartime experience
